idea_text:
Semantic segmentation models can achieve high overlap while relying on non-causal acquisition cues—scanner identity, reconstruction kernel, field of view, embedded overlays, or site-specific preprocessing—that correlate with anatomy or disease in the training set. Domain-adversarial training is the obvious response, but it attempts to remove such information from learned features and cannot establish whether a prediction actually depends on it.

A different approach is to create paired images in which anatomy is held fixed while acquisition provenance is experimentally changed. For raw-data datasets, take one patient’s estimated underlying physical signal and pass it through two or more calibrated forward-and-reconstruction pipelines representing different scanners, sampling patterns, noise levels, and reconstruction kernels. The same physical-space annotation is projected through each pipeline’s geometry. The segmentation model is then constrained to produce the same physical decision after mapping predictions back to the common patient coordinate system. Importantly, consistency is enforced only on regions whose labels remain observable under both acquisitions: a resolution-and-noise test excludes structures for which one pipeline has destroyed the relevant signal. Thus the method does not incorrectly demand invariance when acquisition quality genuinely changes what can be inferred.

The key scientific contribution is an intervention-based test of acquisition causality rather than another invariant architecture. For each acquisition factor, one can estimate the causal effect on segmentation by changing that factor while holding the latent anatomy and all other simulated factors fixed. Training penalizes effects outside the precomputed observability-exclusion regions; evaluation reports both ordinary accuracy and the rate at which irrelevant acquisition interventions change physical-space labels. Real repeat scans or phantom measurements calibrate each forward model and test whether robustness transfers beyond simulation.

The step most likely to degenerate is generating pairs that differ only cosmetically or are physically unrealistic. This is prevented by performing interventions in measurement space, validating simulated measurement and reconstruction statistics against paired scanner or phantom acquisitions, and withholding real cross-scanner repeat scans as the decisive test. The claim is consequently narrow but sound: where two calibrated acquisition processes preserve sufficient evidence for the same annotated structure, prediction changes reveal avoidable dependence on acquisition provenance. This should reduce scanner-driven failures without suppressing legitimate sensitivity to resolution or signal quality.

final_idea_core.core_claim: The method intervenes on acquisition factors in simulation to causally test and penalize model dependence on acquisition provenance, rather than merely removing information adversarially.
final_idea_core.mechanism: It generates paired synthetic images from a single underlying anatomy by simulating different acquisition pipelines, then constrains the segmentation model to produce consistent physical-space predictions across these pairs.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Semantic segmentation models rely on non-causal acquisition cues, leading to performance that doesn't generalize across different scanners or acquisition protocols.
final_idea_core.source_gap: Accurate forward models can be created to simulate diverse acquisition processes and their impact on physical signals and annotations.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: The model's segmentation predictions will exhibit reduced sensitivity to irrelevant acquisition provenance while maintaining legitimate sensitivity to signal quality, leading to more robust generalization across different scanners.

idea_text:
The proposed research is to make low-precision language-model sampling *exact with respect to a full-precision reference policy*, while reading high-precision weights only when the sampled decision is genuinely ambiguous. The initial target is the output projection, where approximation errors directly alter token probabilities and can erase rare reasoning trajectories during reinforcement-learning rollouts.

The obvious approach is to minimize quantization error or assign more bits to “important” weights, then hope downstream behavior is preserved. That controls a surrogate—weight or logit distortion—not the discrete random decision actually used to generate experience. The different causal lever here is to certify each sampled token decision and refine precision only until that decision is provably unchanged.

Store the output matrix as a coarse low-bit matrix plus progressively refinable residual bitplanes. The coarse matrix remains on the GPU; residual bitplanes may reside in slower memory and be cached opportunistically. For an exact backbone hidden state \(h\), each reference logit is

\[
z_i=h^\top(q_i+r_i).
\]

Blockwise residual metadata provides rigorous bounds \(L_i\le z_i\le U_i\), for example from the known maximum omitted residual magnitude and the corresponding blockwise \(\ell_1\)-norms of \(h\). Sampling uses Gumbel-max: draw one reproducible Gumbel value \(g_i\) per vocabulary item and consider intervals \([L_i+g_i,U_i+g_i]\). If one token’s lower endpoint exceeds every other token’s upper endpoint, it is provably the same token that full-precision Gumbel-max would select. Otherwise, fetch another residual bitplane only for rows whose upper bounds can still beat the current best lower bound, tighten their intervals, and repeat. In the worst case all residuals are read and the computation reduces to ordinary full-precision sampling.

This construction gives a hard invariant: every emitted token is exactly the token selected by the reference full-precision policy under the same random draw. Consequently, complete autoregressive trajectories have the same distribution as full-precision trajectories, rather than merely similar perplexity. It can therefore be used for RL rollout generation without quantization silently changing policy entropy, likelihood ratios, reward estimates, or access to low-probability reasoning paths. The stored bitplanes can still be used conventionally when approximate serving is acceptable.

The most likely degeneracy is that interval bounds remain too wide, forcing nearly every row to full precision. The mechanism does not assume this away. First, refinement is monotone and always terminates correctly, so degeneration affects speed but never policy fidelity. Second, whether useful savings exist has a directly measurable condition: at refinement level \(k\), certification succeeds exactly when the gap between the largest perturbed coarse score and all competitors exceeds their remaining certified error radii. Experiments should report the distribution of this certified gap, residual bytes fetched per token, and fallback rate—not only end-to-end speed. Blockwise bounds, reordered bitplanes that reduce the largest residual directions first, and caching affect efficiency but not correctness. A decisive negative result is also well-defined: if real hidden states and Gumbel gaps rarely satisfy the certificate before most residual data are read, exact decision-preserving compression is not beneficial for that model.

The central hypothesis is that most sampled decisions have a clear perturbed-logit winner even when raw token distributions have long tails, so only a small set of competing output rows needs refinement. The key contribution would not be another quantizer, but a serving and rollout procedure that converts compression error from an uncontrolled behavioral perturbation into adaptive memory traffic while preserving the reference policy by construction.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Instead of controlling surrogate metrics like weight or logit distortion, it directly ensures that every sampled token decision is exactly the same as the full-precision reference policy's decision under the same random draw.
final_idea_core.mechanism: It certifies each sampled token decision by adaptively reading progressively more precise weight data (residual bitplanes) only until the sampled decision is provably identical to what a full-precision Gumbel-max sampling would yield.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Low-precision language model sampling introduces approximation errors that subtly alter token probabilities, potentially erasing rare reasoning trajectories during reinforcement learning rollouts.
final_idea_core.source_gap: Most sampled decisions have a clear winner among perturbed logits, even with long-tailed token distributions, allowing for successful certification with only a small subset of competing output rows needing full refinement.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: Every emitted token will exactly match the full-precision policy's choice, resulting in complete autoregressive trajectories having the same distribution, thereby enabling RL rollout generation without quantization silently changing policy behavior, and r…

idea_text:
Language-model reinforcement learning for formal mathematics explores token sequences, although the environment only cares about the proof state produced by those tokens. This creates two opposing errors: thousands of paraphrastic tactic strings can give high token entropy while reaching the same state, and token entropy can collapse even when several substantively different proof steps remain available. The proposed idea is to move the policy’s stochastic choice from text to verifier-defined state transitions.

For theorem proving with a proof assistant, expose a bounded set of primitive actions at each proof state: applying an available theorem, introducing or eliminating a connective, rewriting with an in-scope equality, instantiating a variable from a finite candidate set, or invoking a bounded computation. Each action is executed speculatively by the proof assistant. Invalid actions enter a designated failure outcome; valid actions are grouped whenever the proof assistant reports the same canonical successor state, including identical goals, hypotheses, metavariable assignments, and local context up to alpha-renaming. The language model scores actions using their structured arguments and the current proof state, samples a successor-state class, and only afterward renders a representative action as text if a textual trace is required.

Reinforcement learning then maximizes proof success subject to a minimum conditional entropy over distinct nonfailure successor states at unresolved states. Probability assigned to several actions producing the same successor is summed before entropy is computed. The constraint is imposed only when at least two distinct valid successors exist; otherwise it is exactly zero and creates no artificial pressure. Invalid and state-preserving actions remain in the reward calculation with explicit costs but do not count toward the exploration requirement, preventing the model from satisfying it through syntax errors or no-ops. A primal-dual update can enforce the entropy floor, while ordinary policy gradients optimize return over the sampled transition classes. Because the complete bounded action set is executed before grouping, class probabilities and entropy are computed exactly rather than inferred by a learned semantic model.

The key departure from the obvious approach—adding or preserving token-level entropy—is that exploration is defined on consequences certified by the environment, not on linguistic choices. Under the bounded action language, maintaining positive entropy provably allocates probability to multiple verifier-distinct proof states; paraphrases cannot inflate the exploration measure. Conversely, when only one productive transition exists, the signal correctly degenerates to zero rather than demanding meaningless randomness.

The main empirical question is whether this semantic allocation of rollout budget discovers successful proofs more efficiently than token-space RL. Evaluation should therefore measure not only theorem completion but unique proof states reached per verifier call, coverage of successful proof families, and robustness after controlling for total rollouts and action-set size. The scope is deliberately formal reasoning, where successor-state equivalence is available from a trusted verifier; the proposal does not assume that semantic equivalence can be reliably learned from text.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Exploration is explicitly defined and enforced as a minimum conditional entropy over verifier-distinct nonfailure successor states, rather than on linguistic (token) choices.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The policy's stochastic choice is moved from token sequences to verifier-defined proof state transitions, where primitive actions are executed speculatively and grouped by their canonical successor states.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Traditional language model reinforcement learning for formal mathematics suffers from exploration inefficiency due to focusing on token-level entropy, which conflates paraphrastic variations with genuinely distinct proof steps.
final_idea_core.source_gap: A trusted proof assistant can precisely and efficiently identify canonical equivalence between proof states resulting from different action sequences within a bounded action set.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: This semantic exploration strategy will discover successful proofs more efficiently, evidenced by higher theorem completion rates, more unique proof states reached per verifier call, and broader coverage of proof families, compared to token-space RL.

idea_text:
Many mathematical RL tasks provide only a final-answer reward. The resulting credit assignment is extremely sparse, while learned process-reward models can be confidently wrong and full formalization demands expensive proof annotations. A different approach is to restrict attention initially to algebraic reasoning and make each generated solution *self-checking through randomized identity tests*.

The policy must represent its derivation as a sequence of expression rewrites. Each step states that the current rational or polynomial expression is equal to a proposed next expression; the final expression must directly encode the submitted answer. During training, an evaluator substitutes secret random values from a large finite field into both sides of every rewrite. It rejects substitutions at denominator poles and repeats the test across independently chosen fields and points. The reward is the verified fraction of the derivation, capped by an exact final-answer check. Thus a model receives dense credit for reaching a correct intermediate expression even if it later fails.

This is not merely consistency checking. For expressions of bounded degree, a false polynomial identity passes one test with probability at most \(d/|F|\) by polynomial identity testing; multiple independent tests make accidental acceptance negligible. Rational identities reduce to polynomial identities by cross-multiplication after checking nonzero denominators. Random primes prevent identities that happen to hold only modulo one characteristic. Concrete numerical rewrites are checked exactly rather than randomized. Unsupported operations—inequalities, transcendental functions, or unbounded iteration—receive no intermediate reward, making the initial claim deliberately narrower rather than relying on an unsound heuristic.

The main degeneracy risk is reward farming with unrelated tautologies. The interface prevents this structurally: every accepted step must consume the previous expression and replace it with an equivalent next expression, and only progress along this single chain toward the final answer is rewarded. Repeating an expression earns no additional credit, while expression size and step count are bounded. Secret evaluation points are resampled after generation, so the policy cannot tailor claims to known tests.

The research hypothesis is that verifier-grounded prefix rewards will let RL discover long algebraic derivations with substantially fewer rollouts than outcome-only training, without inheriting a learned judge’s errors. The key comparison is against final-answer RL, learned process rewards, and symbolic simplifiers on held-out problems, measuring solution accuracy, verified progress before failure, reward false-positive rate, and robustness to adversarially constructed invalid identities. The conceptual shift is from estimating whether reasoning *looks correct* to using an interactive-proof technique that gives each algebraic step a quantifiable soundness guarantee.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Instead of training a separate reward model or relying on full formalization, the solution's internal steps are made self-checking via robust polynomial identity testing.
final_idea_core.mechanism: Each algebraic rewrite step is validated by randomized identity tests using secret numerical substitutions from large finite fields, providing dense, verifiable prefix rewards.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Sparse rewards in mathematical RL tasks with only final-answer feedback hinder learning of long algebraic derivations.
final_idea_core.source_gap: The probability of a false algebraic identity passing multiple independent randomized tests is negligibly small for bounded-degree expressions.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: Verifier-grounded prefix rewards will enable RL to discover long algebraic derivations with substantially fewer rollouts and higher accuracy than outcome-only training or learned process rewards.

idea_text:
A major weakness of reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning is that outcome rewards cannot distinguish learning a reusable solution method from exploiting instance-specific regularities, memorized benchmark answers, or brittle shortcuts. The obvious response—use more held-out problems or a learned process verifier—only tests additional fixed instances or introduces another model whose judgments can be exploited.

Instead, train the model to output an executable solver for a parameterized family of problems, not merely an answer to the displayed instance. Each training problem is produced by a generator with a large parameter space and an exact answer oracle. The model receives one instance and emits a sandboxed program that accepts any instance in the same documented format. The program is committed before evaluation. Only then does the verifier privately sample several new parameter settings from the same family, execute the committed program on the original and hidden sibling instances, and compare every result with the oracle. The reward can initially be the fraction passed for usable learning signal, while final-stage training and evaluation require all challenges to pass within fixed time and memory limits.

This changes what one rollout establishes. If a submitted program is correct on only a fraction \(p\) of the family distribution, its probability of passing \(k\) independent hidden challenges is \(p^k\). Thus an instance-specific shortcut with small coverage is suppressed exponentially without relying on a learned assessment of reasoning quality. Challenges must be sampled after commitment so the model cannot tailor its program to them. The sandbox excludes network access, stored answer tables, the oracle, and generator internals; randomized generation uses a domain too large for enumeration. Producing a genuinely general algorithm—even one recalled from pretraining—is acceptable because reusable problem solving is precisely the target behavior.

Training would compare this interactive reward against ordinary answer-only reinforcement learning using disjoint generator seeds and separately implemented test generators. Primary measurements would be hidden-family pass rate, robustness as the parameter range expands, and transfer to families with the same mathematical structure but different surface representations. Natural-language solutions can be generated afterward, but they are not trusted as evidence of correctness.

The signal’s main possible degeneracy is a problem family whose sibling instances share no recoverable structure, making generalization impossible, or whose generator leaks shortcuts. The method therefore applies only to families with a declared common specification and an exact oracle, and uses adversarially varied serialization plus independently written evaluation generators. It does not claim to cover arbitrary olympiad problems. Within this scoped setting, however, reward validity follows from executable behavior on post-commitment random challenges rather than from token entropy, process annotation, or an evaluator model’s judgment.

final_idea_core.core_claim: The model's submitted solver program is evaluated against multiple hidden instances from the same problem family, sampled *after* the program's commitment, to exponentially suppress instance-specific shortcuts.
final_idea_core.mechanism: Train a model to output an executable solver program for a parameterized family of problems, not just an instance's answer, and evaluate it on new, hidden instances from that family.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning struggles to distinguish general solution methods from instance-specific shortcuts and memorization due to outcome rewards.
final_idea_core.source_gap: Problem families exist whose sibling instances share recoverable, generalizable structure, and whose generators do not inadvertently leak exploitable shortcuts.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: Models will exhibit significantly higher hidden-family pass rates, improved robustness to expanded parameter ranges, and better transfer to structurally similar problems, indicating true generalization rather than shortcut exploitation.

idea_text:
A major failure in reasoning RL is that exploration is measured at the point where text is sampled, even though many different prefixes lead to the same downstream behavior while a low-probability prefix may uniquely make a correct answer reachable. Increasing token entropy therefore spends rollouts on paraphrases without preserving prefixes that have genuine future option value.

Instead of rewarding entropy, allocate rollout compute according to whether a prefix changes the distribution of verifier outcomes obtainable from its continuations. At selected branch points, sample several candidate prefixes. For each prefix, generate a small panel of independent continuations and record only externally observable outcomes: final-answer equivalence class, verifier error category, tool execution result, timeout, or success. This produces an empirical outcome distribution for each prefix. Continue expanding a subset chosen to maximize coverage of distinct outcome distributions, while reserving some samples for statistical uncertainty. RL updates remain ordinary outcome-reward updates; this mechanism changes which trajectories are collected, not their rewards or policy-gradient target. Because branching reuses the shared key-value cache, the additional computation is concentrated after decision points rather than duplicating entire rollouts.

The key causal move is to treat exploration as preservation of prefixes with different reachable futures, not as uncertainty over their next tokens. Two linguistically different derivations that induce indistinguishable verifier-outcome distributions receive no diversity benefit. Conversely, a rare prefix is retained when its continuations reach outcomes unavailable from common prefixes, even if none has yet succeeded. This is discontinuous from the obvious approach of adding entropy bonuses or clustering text embeddings: the diversity signal is defined by downstream intervention—complete each prefix repeatedly and observe what becomes reachable.

Outcome-distribution differences are estimated with multinomial confidence sets. A prefix is eliminated only when its confidence set is contained within that of already retained prefixes up to a specified tolerance; otherwise it remains eligible for expansion. Final policy-gradient samples are accompanied by their known branching-selection probabilities and corrected by inverse-probability weighting, or used only with an on-policy objective conditioned on the selected branch, preventing the rollout scheduler from silently biasing the claimed policy objective.

The most likely degeneracy is that all early continuations fail identically, producing an all-zero signal. The outcome alphabet must therefore include deterministic verifier states short of success—such as parse validity, distinct executable outputs, constraint-violation vectors, and failure locations—not learned judgments. If the available verifier truly returns only one undifferentiated failure symbol, the method explicitly falls back to uniform branching and claims no advantage; it does not manufacture diversity from text. The central hypothesis is testable: at equal rollout cost, future-outcome-directed branching should discover more distinct successful solution families and achieve higher pass rates than token-entropy regularization, embedding-based diversity, or uniform tree expansion, particularly where successful reasoning depends on an early low-probability commitment.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Define 'diversity' and 'option value' not by text embeddings or token entropy, but by the dissimilarity of empirical outcome distributions obtained from repeatedly completing candidate prefixes.
final_idea_core.mechanism: Allocate rollout compute by selecting prefixes that maximize the diversity of their empirically observed downstream verifier outcome distributions, rather than the entropy of their next tokens.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Current reasoning RL exploration methods waste computational resources by promoting linguistic diversity (high token entropy) that does not necessarily lead to genuinely different downstream outcomes or preserve prefixes critical for rare successful solut…
final_idea_core.source_gap: The available verifier can produce sufficiently differentiated, deterministic intermediate and terminal outcomes to distinguish prefixes, even when full success is rare, without manufacturing diversity from linguistic variations.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: At equal rollout cost, this method will discover more distinct successful solution families and achieve higher pass rates, especially for problems requiring early low-probability commitments, compared to token-entropy, embedding-based diversity, or unifor…

idea_text:
Many exact-answer reasoning tasks provide only a binary reward, even when a model has computed substantial but incomplete information about the answer. A wrong 100-digit integer and an integer wrong in only one component are indistinguishable. The obvious response is a learned process reward or digit-level supervision, but both impose an arbitrary representation of progress and can reward plausible-looking mistakes.

For problems whose answer is a bounded integer, train the policy to return the answer simultaneously through several independently checkable modular views. For each rollout, the evaluator samples fresh, pairwise-coprime small primes and asks for the answer’s residue modulo each prime, followed by a single integer answer. Each residue receives an exact binary reward from the known answer or executable verifier. The final integer receives reward only if it is both correct and congruent with every submitted residue. The primes are resampled across rollouts, so the model cannot memorize a fixed encoding.

This converts one extremely sparse event into several easier, mathematically exact events. A trajectory that correctly determines parity, divisibility structure, or low-modulus arithmetic can receive valid credit without pretending that its full answer is correct. As competence grows, use more primes and larger moduli. Once their product exceeds twice the certified answer bound, the complete residue vector uniquely determines the integer within that range by the Chinese remainder theorem. Thus, success on all modular components is not a heuristic proxy: together with the range check, it is equivalent to recovering the exact answer.

The central intervention is not ordinary reward shaping. It changes the answer interface into independently verifiable projections whose conjunction preserves the original task exactly. To prevent a policy from collecting modular reward while never learning reconstruction, training batches should mix three mechanically distinct obligations: predict individual residues, reconstruct the integer from supplied correct residues, and jointly produce residues plus the integer. Reconstruction examples can be generated without reasoning annotations, and the consistency check prevents contradictory outputs from receiving final-answer credit. At evaluation, only the ordinary integer answer is required.

The most likely degeneration is modular shortcut learning: the model might solve each small-modulus problem independently but fail to recover the integer. The explicit reconstruction obligation addresses this directly, and the key diagnostic is therefore not residue accuracy alone but reconstruction accuracy as the modulus product crosses the uniqueness threshold. A decisive experiment would compare equal-compute outcome-only RL, digit-prefix rewards, and this interface on bounded large-integer problems, measuring exact-answer accuracy, reconstruction from unseen prime sets, and transfer back to the standard single-integer interface. The predicted gain is strongest where full answers are rarely sampled but partial modular computations are already within the policy’s reach.

final_idea_core.core_claim: The answer interface is modified to incorporate independently verifiable modular projections whose conjunction, via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, is mathematically equivalent to the exact integer answer within a bounded range.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The model is trained to simultaneously output the integer answer and its residues modulo several independently sampled, pairwise-coprime primes, with each residue receiving binary reward.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Sparse binary rewards in exact-answer integer reasoning tasks prevent models from receiving credit for substantial but incomplete progress.
final_idea_core.source_gap: The model can learn to perform accurate modular arithmetic and also integrate this information to reconstruct the full integer more effectively than direct end-to-end training.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: Models will achieve higher exact-answer accuracy on bounded large-integer problems by receiving more granular, mathematically sound reward signals for partial computations, and will demonstrate better reconstruction ability from unseen prime sets.

idea_text:
Quantized reinforcement learning usually optimizes the behavior of the quantized model and merely hopes that this is a good proxy for the intended full-precision policy. Small numerical errors can alter rollout probabilities and policy gradients, especially for rare reasoning paths. The obvious response is to reduce quantization error or occasionally train at full precision. Instead, use quantized training only as a computational approximation while constructing an estimator whose expectation is exactly the full-precision policy gradient.

Create a fixed ladder of weight precisions ending at the original model precision. Let \(g_\ell\) denote an unbiased on-policy gradient estimate for the RL objective when rollouts and log-probabilities are both computed at precision level \(\ell\). Then the desired full-precision gradient satisfies the finite telescoping identity
\[
\mathbb E[g_L]
=\mathbb E[g_0]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb E[g_\ell-g_{\ell-1}].
\]
At every update, compute the inexpensive lowest-precision gradient. Randomly choose how far up the precision ladder to evaluate, and for every selected level compute the paired difference \(g_\ell-g_{\ell-1}\), divided by that level’s probability of being selected. Summing these terms gives an exactly unbiased estimator of the full-precision gradient. The two members of each difference use the same prompts, random token draws represented by shared uniforms, and other random seeds to reduce variance; each policy’s score-function term is nevertheless evaluated under its own generated trajectory, so coupling does not introduce an off-policy substitution. Full-precision weights may be streamed only for the rare highest-level correction rather than kept resident throughout training.

The key distinction from mixed-precision heuristics is that low precision is not treated as the target policy. Quantization bias cancels algebraically in expectation, regardless of whether quantization errors are normally distributed, low rank, or harmless to most token decisions. Precision-level sampling probabilities are chosen from pilot estimates of the second moments and costs of the paired corrections, minimizing estimator variance under a compute budget. A conventional full-precision gradient minibatch remains a valid special case, but the proposed estimator gains whenever adjacent-precision gradients are strongly coupled and their differences shrink with precision.

The most likely degeneration is explosive correction variance when a small logit perturbation causes paired autoregressive trajectories to diverge. This does not invalidate unbiasedness, but could erase the compute advantage. The design therefore measures correction second moments directly and assigns every level a nonzero sampling probability; levels with large corrections are sampled frequently or merged into the base precision. Gradient clipping must not be applied separately to correction terms because that would destroy unbiasedness; any required bounded influence should instead be part of the explicitly defined target objective. If measured correction variance does not decay, the method reports that low precision offers no statistically valid saving rather than silently optimizing a different policy.

The central experiment would compare this estimator against full-precision RL and ordinary quantized RL at matched expected compute. Besides reasoning accuracy, evaluation should measure gradient bias against high-sample full-precision references, correction variance by level, and the frequency with which rare high-precision corrections reverse an apparent low-precision update. The predicted result is full-precision learning behavior in expectation at substantially lower average memory traffic and computation when precision corrections decay, without assuming that quantized rollouts are behaviorally equivalent to full-precision ones.
